# ordo amoris: the order of loves — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

> the order of loves. Augustine's account of virtue as rightly ordered love: a good will is one that loves things in proportion to their worth, God first, then creatures in their proper measure, and none of them as though it were the highest good.

Glossary

## ordo amoris

the order of loves

Latin · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / ordo amoris

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Love](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/love) · [God](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/god) · [Desire](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/desire) · [Good](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/good) · [Morality](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/morality) · [Order](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/order) · [Will](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/will)

### What the term does

Augustine's account of virtue as rightly ordered love: a good will is one that loves things in proportion to their worth, God first, then creatures in their proper measure, and none of them as though it were the highest good. The concept is Augustinian rather than directly scriptural, and it was developed before him in Ambrose and in the Neoplatonic hierarchy of goods. It underlies the later Christian analysis of sin as disordered love rather than as the pursuit of evil, and it is why Augustine treats the Fall as a matter of what is loved rather than of what is known.

### The reading the sources do not support

Reduced to 'love the right things', which loses the proportional structure. What makes the doctrine do work is that a love can be too great as well as misplaced, and the sin can lie in the degree rather than the object.
